titre: The More Serious the Charge, the Less the Accused Could Defend Himself
accroche: Until 1836, a man accused of theft could pay a lawyer to defend him at trial. A man accused of murder could not: English law left him alone before the jury.
contenu_vulgarise:
In an English courtroom of the 1830s, a man accused of stealing cattle could have a lawyer represent him, questioning the witnesses and pleading before the jury in his place. A few yards away, in the same room, a man accused of murder had no such right: the law refused to let a lawyer address the court for him, even if he had paid for one to assist him in silence. The graver the charge, the less the accused could defend himself.

## An Inverted Hierarchy

The rule came from medieval English law: in a trial for felony (the gravest crimes, punished by death or transportation), the accused had to conduct his own defense before the jury. The thinking was that an innocent man needed no one to tell the truth, and that a lawyer would only bring artifice where the facts alone should speak. Those accused of misdemeanor, lesser offenses, were subject to no such rule and had long been allowed to be defended.

On July 14, 1836, during the debate on the bill in the House of Lords, Lord Lyndhurst piles up his own examples: a foreigner just arrived, unable to follow the proceedings in a language he does not understand; a deaf and mute man, to whom a judge nonetheless says, as to every defendant in a felony, that no lawyer may speak for him. He closes his speech by reading an essay published by an anonymous dignitary of the Church of England, which describes the same sentence inflicted on a poor fifteen-year-old girl, a foreigner, a deaf person, a stammerer, the infirm, the blind, the aged. The Lord Chancellor himself points out the inconsistency of the system: the law allows a lawyer to speak for a man accused of treason, the worst of charges, and for a mere misdemeanant, the least serious, and only felony, in between, is denied it.

## What the 1836 Act Corrects

The Trials for Felony Act, which received royal assent on August 20, 1836 and came into force on October 1 of that year, for the first time allows anyone accused of felony to be defended “by counsel or attorney,” that is, to have a lawyer speak in his name before the jury, and not merely at his side. The Act does not create a right to a lawyer. It extends it, repairing an anomaly in which the most severely punished crime was precisely the one where professional defense was most lacking.

## What the Chronology Teaches

The idea that the right to counsel in criminal cases is an ancient given of Anglo-American law does not survive this date: in 1836, the common law had protected those accused of minor offenses for centuries, yet let a man accused of murder speak alone for his life. The content of the right had long been known elsewhere in the system. What shifts is the order in which it appeared: the most necessary protection is not always the first one granted.

citation.texte: Your counsel cannot speak for you, you must speak for yourself.
citation.auteur: An anonymous dignitary of the Church of England, quoted by Lord Lyndhurst
citation.source: Essay read at the close of the debate on the Prisoners' Counsel Bill, House of Lords, July 14, 1836 (Hansard)

carte.punch: A murder suspect pleaded alone; a mere misdemeanant already had a lawyer.
carte.idee: Until 1836, English law forbade a lawyer from speaking for a man accused of felony, the gravest crime, while already allowing it for minor offenses and for treason. The most necessary protection was not the first one granted.

quiz.question: Before the 1836 Act, what was the situation of a person accused of felony (the gravest crimes) in an English court?
choix: He could choose a lawyer, but the lawyer had to plead in Latin before the judge
He had to conduct his own defense before the jury, with no lawyer allowed to speak for him
He was not entitled to any trial, his sentence being fixed directly by the judge
He could be represented, but only by a member of his family
quiz.explication: The common-law rule required a person accused of felony to speak for himself before the jury, with no lawyer able to question witnesses or plead in his place. Those accused of minor offenses, though less serious, were subject to no such restriction.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What inconsistency does the Lord Chancellor point out in the debate of July 14, 1836?
choix: The law allowed accused women to be defended by a lawyer, but never men
The law reserved defense by counsel for those accused who could afford the fees
The law allowed a lawyer to speak for treason and for a mere misdemeanor, but not for felony in between
The law imposed a court-appointed lawyer on every accused person, even those who did not want one
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Lord Chancellor notes that the law already allowed a lawyer to speak for a man accused of treason, the worst of charges, and for a mere misdemeanant, the least serious, with only felony in between being denied it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What examples does Lord Lyndhurst himself draw in his speech to illustrate the injustice of the rule?
choix: A foreigner unable to follow the proceedings in a language he does not understand, and a deaf and mute man
A fifteen-year-old girl and a blind old man, cited in the essay he reads at the close
A nobleman wrongly convicted and a man pardoned after his execution
A ten-year-old child and a pregnant woman, tried before the same court
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Lord Lyndhurst builds the examples of the foreigner and the deaf and mute man himself; the fifteen-year-old girl and the blind old man come from the essay of an anonymous clergyman that he then reads at the close.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does the Trials for Felony Act of 1836 do, according to the entry?
choix: It creates for the first time a right to counsel in criminal cases, previously unknown to English law
It abolishes the popular jury in favor of judgment by a single magistrate
It abolishes the death penalty for all crimes classed as felony in England
It extends to those accused of felony the right to be defended by a lawyer, already granted to others
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1836 Act does not create a right to a lawyer: it extends it to those accused of felony, who had been denied it until then while other categories of accused already enjoyed it.
